narrative:
The model estimates a 70% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key aspects of your professional profile that, according to patterns seen across many similar employees, signal higher turnover risk.

Your total years of experience emerged as the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting you will leave. With 6–10 years overall, you sit in a mid-career range where many people begin exploring new opportunities; only 34.9% of employees the model expected to stay fall into this bracket, compared with half who have just 1–5 years.

Next, the model noted that you have not received any external job offers while at your current organization. Surprisingly, this absence of outside interest actually increased the predicted likelihood of leaving. In the group of employees expected to stay, far more people also lacked alternative offers, suggesting the model sees your situation as one where internal dissatisfaction may eventually drive departure even without visible external pull.

Your tenure in your present role (1–5 years) was the third most influential factor and further tilted the prediction toward leaving. This relatively short time with the organization, shared by about half of those predicted to stay, appears to signal that you are still in an early adjustment phase where commitment levels can remain uncertain.

The organization should consider discussing your long-term career goals with you and exploring whether additional responsibilities, clearer advancement paths, or improved recognition could strengthen your connection to the company. You may also wish to reflect on what would make staying feel more rewarding.
